story: In 1978, NASA astrophysicist Donald Kessler warned that humanity could accidentally trap itself on Earth. His mathematical model revealed a grim tipping point: past a critical density of satellites and spent rocket boosters, orbital crashes would trigger a chain reaction. One collision would shatter spacecraft into thousands of high-speed fragments, each becoming an untrackable bullet that causes further collisions. Even if all rocket launches ceased tomorrow, the debris cloud would continue multiplying on its own, rendering key orbits unusable for centuries. This is not science fiction. In 2007, an anti-satellite missile test blasted a Chinese weather satellite into over 3,000 fragments. Two years later, a dead Russian military satellite smashed into an active Iridium satellite at 26,000 miles per hour, generating thousands more orbital projectiles. In 2021, another missile test sent ISS astronauts scrambling into escape capsules. Orbit is filling up, and the slow-motion cascade may already be underway.
angle: Once orbital debris crosses a critical threshold, collisions will multiply automatically for centuries even if humanity never launches another rocket.
disputed: Whether the Kessler syndrome has already begun: Some studies and models indicate that low Earth orbit has already crossed the critical instability threshold where debris accumulates autonomously, whereas other orbital dynamics experts argue that discrete fragmentations still dominate and runaway cascading has not yet started. Scripts should attribute this: 'according to some debris models, while other researchers maintain runaway cascading has not yet begun.'

Date of the first major satellite collision: EarthSky states the collision between an operating and defunct satellite happened in 2006, whereas Orbital Radar, SpaceDaily, SpaceNexus, and Aerospace America date the Cosmos 2251 and Iridium 33 collision to February 10, 2009. Scripts should follow the consensus 2009 date and omit 2006.
